To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) most studies show that spring arrival is earlier, while departure time varies between studies and between individuals, and (2) most studies show no change in BART, while the few studies that do show a change, show that BART is either earlier or later, and that the direction of the shift is related to whether the individual arrives early or late.

(1) phenological shifts in migratory birds are most pronounced in the first half of the migration season, (2) phenological shifts vary between species and between individual timing of migration, and (3) the timing of the second half of the season, i.e. departure, shows large variation between species.

(i) the choice of species and measurement of migration timing is important when studying phenological changes; (ii) there is a general trend of earlier spring arrival, but the timing of autumn migration varies according to species and individual; (iii) the timing of autumn departure is not likely to change the breeding ecology of individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the phenology of bird migration changes in response to global warming.
the phenology of avians’ migration and how it is changing in response to a changing climate.
the question of how phenology of migratory birds has changed in the last 20 years.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the majority of the studied migratory songbirds have advanced their spring migration and that the changes in the timing of migration have occurred in the early arriving and late departing individuals.
the timing of migration has changed in the direction of earlier arrival and later departure for most songbird species in Europe, but the changes are not uniform across species.
most species show a shift to earlier spring arrival, and that the timing of migration has changed in most species but that the timing of the BART is less likely to have changed in most species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
while most individuals do not change their BART, the phenology of the whole population has changed.
most of the variation in migration timing is explained by the choice of species, and that the timing of migration has changed in most species.
the changes in phenology of migratory birds are more complex than previously thought and that the effects on population dynamics are likely to be small.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the phenological changes in migration of migratory birds can vary between species and that this variation can be explained by differences in the timing and duration of migration.

the phenology of bird migration is complex, and that it is important to consider the specific species and the specific measurement used when comparing results between studies and making predictions of future changes.
the choice of species and the choice of measurements are crucial for the conclusions drawn.
